title: CR7 vs LM10 in python
text:
Question and scope
How do Ronaldo and Messi compare in the number and types of club goals recorded in this dataset? Each row represents one goal, not one match. The file is a historical snapshot, so these results are not current career totals.

title: CR7 vs LM10 in python
text:
Count goals and check coverage
I count rows for each player and check the earliest and latest dates. Different coverage periods mean the totals should not be interpreted as a fair comparison of scoring rates.

summary = stats.groupby("Player").agg(
    recorded_goals=("Player", "size"),
    first_date=("Date", "min"),
    last_date=("Date", "max"),
    missing_goal_type=("Type", lambda column: column.isna().sum()),
)

title: CR7 vs LM10 in python
text:
Compare scoring types
Missing goal types remain in an explicit Unknown category. Percentages use every recorded goal for each player as the denominator, including unknown types.

stats["Type"] = stats["Type"].fillna("Unknown")
type_counts = pd.crosstab(stats["Type"], stats["Player"])
type_percent = type_counts.div(type_counts.sum(axis=0), axis=1) * 100
type_percent.round(1).rename_axis("Goal type")

Visualize the distribution

title: CR7 vs LM10 in python
text:
What I found
Messi’s largest category is left-footed shots (436 goals), while Ronaldo’s is right-footed shots (253). Ronaldo also has more recorded headers (112 versus 24). These differences describe the scoring profiles in this file; they do not measure shooting accuracy because unsuccessful attempts are absent.
The categories mix body parts with situations such as penalties and free kicks. A goal labelled Penalty is not also counted under the foot used, so these categories cannot establish the total number of goals scored with each foot. There are also 15 unknown types for Ronaldo and one for Messi.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Starting MDS at UBC honestly feels a little strange in a good way. I already know the campus, but being here as a new grad student makes everything feel fresh again. The program moves pretty fast, so there’s definitely a bit of pressure, but I’m also excited to meet new people, learn more practical data science skills, and see what this year is going to be like. It feels like a new start without actually having to start completely from zero.
Imagine Day was probably one of the best ways to ease into the new school year. Campus was super busy, with booths, music, events, and students everywhere. I spent some time walking around, checking out different clubs, and just enjoying the atmosphere. Even though I’ve been at UBC for a while, it was still fun seeing campus feel so alive again. It made the start of the semester feel a lot less serious and a lot more exciting.
I know MDS is going to be a busy year, and I’ll probably be spending a lot of time on assignments and projects, but I still want to enjoy the student side of UBC too. I want to go to more events, meet people outside my program, and actually make time for the fun stuff instead of only thinking about school. It’s only the beginning, but so far, I’m excited for what’s coming next.

title: CR7 vs LM10 in R
text:
Question and scope
Do the players have different scoring profiles in this historical club-goal dataset? I use R to count the recorded goals and compare the proportion scored at home and away. Each row is one goal, so these are not counts of matches or scoring rates per appearance.

title: CR7 vs LM10 in R

Load and inspect the data
The setup suppresses package startup messages while leaving analysis code and output visible. knitr formats the generated tables.

library(knitr)
stats <- read.csv("../../data/mds521_cr7_lm10.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stats$Date <- as.Date(stats$Date)

title: CR7 vs LM10 in R
text:
Summarize goals and date coverage
I split the data by player to check whether the time spans are comparable before interpreting totals.

by_player <- split(stats, stats$Player)
summary_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(by_player), function(player) {
  goals <- by_player[[player]]
  data.frame(
    Player = player,
    Goals = nrow(goals),
    First_date = min(goals$Date),
    Last_date = max(goals$Date)
  )
}))
kable(summary_table, row.names = FALSE)

title: CR7 vs LM10 in R
text:
Compare home and away goals
I inspect the venue codes before calculating percentages. Each player’s denominator is their total number of recorded goals, not their number of home or away matches.

stopifnot(!anyNA(stats$Venue), all(stats$Venue %in% c("H", "A")))
stats$Venue_label <- factor(stats$Venue, levels = c("H", "A"),
                            labels = c("Home", "Away"))
venue_counts <- table(stats$Player, stats$Venue_label)
venue_percent <- prop.table(venue_counts, margin = 1) * 100
kable(venue_counts, caption = "Recorded goals by player and venue.")

Visualize the venue comparison

        col = c("#2166ac", "#b35806"),
        ylim = c(0, 100), ylab = "Share of recorded goals (%)",
        xlab = "Venue", border = NA)

Figure 1: Home and away shares of each player’s recorded club goals. These percentages do not adjust for matches played at each venue.

title: CR7 vs LM10 in R
text:
What I found
In this snapshot, Ronaldo scored 404 goals at home and 306 away. Messi scored 419 at home and 284 away. The home shares are 56.9% and 59.6%, respectively.
This comparison shows where the recorded goals occurred. It cannot establish a home advantage or compare player ability: we would need match appearances, minutes played, and opponent information for both scoring and non-scoring matches. Different career coverage and competitions also limit the comparison.
